questions.prompt: What is a coefficient in a chemical equation?
options: The number in front of a formula that counts how many units react
The small number inside a formula
The arrow between reactants and products
questions.explanation: A coefficient is the big number in front of a formula, counting whole units of the substance.
questions.misconception: The small number inside a formula is a subscript (it counts atoms within one unit) — the coefficient is specifically the number in FRONT.

options: Every atom in the formula — 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens
Only the first atom in the formula
questions.explanation: A coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula it fronts: 2H₂O = 2×2 = 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens.
questions.misconception: The coefficient multiplies the ENTIRE formula, not just part of it — every atom gets multiplied, which is why 2H₂O has four hydrogens.

questions.prompt: How is a coefficient different from a subscript?
options: Coefficient counts units (front); subscript counts atoms (inside)
Coefficient counts atoms; subscript counts units
questions.explanation: The coefficient in front counts whole molecules/units; the subscript inside counts atoms within one formula unit.
questions.misconception: The two numbers play opposite roles — the coefficient multiplies the whole unit while the subscript describes one unit's internal atoms.

questions.prompt: Why do we choose coefficients when balancing an equation?
options: So the atoms on the left match the atoms on the right
To make the equation look longer
questions.explanation: Choosing the right coefficients makes every atom's count equal on both sides — enforcing conservation of mass.
questions.misconception: Balancing never changes what elements react — it only adjusts the NUMBER of each unit so the atom counts match.
